title: The Morning After the Rumour
excerpt: Workplace Romance · Forbidden Attraction · Slow Burn · Mature Romance
content:
The trouble began with a photograph.

It appeared in the restaurant's staff group chat at 8:13 on Monday morning.

The image showed Naomi and Devraj leaving the restaurant where they had eaten dinner. Their hands were linked, and Naomi was laughing at something he had said.

The photograph was harmless.

The comments beneath it were not.

By the time Naomi arrived for her shift, three people had asked whether she was dating the sommelier, two had made jokes about preferential treatment, and one had suggested that Devraj's recent schedule changes were evidence of something improper.

Naomi felt the old fear return so quickly that it made her dizzy.

She found Devraj near the wine station.

"Did you see the photograph?"

"Yes."

"And?"

"And we're holding hands in a photograph."

"Don't make jokes."

"I'm not."

She lowered her voice.

"People are already talking about our work."

His expression changed.

"Has anyone said something directly to you?"

"Not yet. But they will."

"We can talk to the manager before rumours turn into something worse."

"No."

He stared at her.

"No?"

"I don't want to make this official. I don't want everybody involved in my private life. I don't want another relationship turning into a staff meeting."

"Naomi, I'm not asking you to announce anything."

"But they're already watching us."

"And we can't control what people say."

She folded her arms.

"You don't understand."

"Then help me understand."

The gentleness in his voice almost undid her.

She looked away.

"When my last relationship ended, everyone knew about the arguments. Everyone had an opinion about who was right and who was wrong. I couldn't walk into my own kitchen without feeling as though I had to defend myself."

Devraj stepped closer.

"I'm not your ex."

"I know that."

"Do you?"

The question landed harder than she expected.

She looked at him, hurt flashing across her face.

He immediately softened.

"I'm sorry. That came out wrong."

"No. Maybe it came out exactly right."

She took a breath.

"I can't do this if every difficult moment becomes a test of whether I trust you enough."

"And I can't do it if you decide we're finished every time somebody else gets an opinion."

For several seconds, neither spoke.

Then the head manager called Naomi into the office.

The meeting was brief but uncomfortable. The manager had received complaints that the two of them might be favouring each other. There was no evidence of misconduct, but the restaurant had policies about workplace relationships, particularly where scheduling and supervisory responsibilities were involved.

Naomi explained that she was responsible for the kitchen, while Devraj worked on the floor. They did not share a direct reporting line, and neither had received special treatment.

The manager listened.

"I don't mind adults having private lives," she said. "I do mind staff believing that private relationships affect professional decisions. Keep things transparent where necessary, and don't let personal disagreements interfere with service."

Naomi left the office feeling exposed.

Devraj was waiting in the corridor.

"What happened?"

"Nothing dramatic. We're expected to act professionally."

"That seems reasonable."

She stared at him.

"How do you do that?"

"Do what?"

"Make everything sound so easy."

He considered her.

"It isn't easy. I'm just trying not to make it harder than it needs to be."

She wanted to believe him.

But the photograph had made their private happiness feel public, fragile, and suddenly vulnerable to people who knew nothing about them.

During service, Naomi became all business.

She addressed Devraj as she addressed everyone else. She avoided unnecessary conversations. When he brought a plate to the pass, she checked it without meeting his eyes.

He respected the distance.

That somehow hurt more.

At the end of the night, Naomi found him alone near the service entrance, putting on his coat.

"Are you leaving?"

"I thought that would be best."

The words sounded like an accusation, although she knew they weren't meant to.

She swallowed.

"Devraj, I didn't mean for this to happen."

"Neither did I."

He looked tired.

"I care about you, Naomi. But I don't want you to feel trapped by me, and I don't want to spend every day guessing whether you're going to regret being with me."

She stared at him, unable to find an answer that didn't sound like fear.

He continued, quietly.

"I can give you space. I can keep our relationship private. I can follow whatever boundaries we agree on. But I can't pretend I don't care just because other people have noticed."

Her eyes burned.

"I need time."

He nodded.

"All right."

She had expected him to argue.

Instead, he opened the door and stepped into the cold night.

"Goodnight, Naomi."

"Goodnight."

The door closed behind him.

She stood alone in the service corridor, listening to the distant hum of the refrigerators.

Above the pass, her handwritten rule remained taped to the wall.

For two years, it had kept her from being hurt by someone she worked beside.

Now, standing in the quiet restaurant, she realised it had also kept her from learning how to stay when something mattered.

She took the rule down.

She didn't tear it up.

Not yet.

She folded it carefully and placed it in the drawer beneath her station.

Then she took out her phone.

She typed a message to Devraj, deleted it, and typed another.

I don't want to lose you. I just don't know how to do this without being afraid.

This time, she pressed send.

His reply came several minutes later.

Then we learn. Slowly. Together, if you still want that.

Naomi read the message twice.

For the first time that night, she allowed herself to cry.

Not because she thought she had lost him.

Because he was giving her the chance to choose him without pretending she wasn't afraid.
